East Kilbride.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of East Kilbride and South Lanarkshire
s1loc: East Kilbride anchors its visitor appeal on the National Museum of Rural Life at Wester Kittochside, a working farm tracing Scotland's agricultural past with historic tractors, traditional farmhouses and tractor-and-trailer rides out to the fields. Calderglen Country Park draws crowds to its wooded gorge along the Rotten Calder, with a small zoo of owls, meerkats and wallabies, ornamental gardens and miles of riverside trails on the edge of town.

The leisure and activity layer centres on James Hamilton Heritage Park, where a 16-acre loch hosts windsurfing, power-boating, kayaking and open-water swimming beside picnic lawns and lochside strolls. The Category A listed Dollan Aqua Centre keeps its landmark 50-metre pool busy through the year, while nearby Whitelee Windfarm, the UK's largest onshore wind farm, opens miles of moorland walking and cycling routes for activity operators.

Heritage and culture run through the East Kilbride Arts Centre and a town built as Scotland's first post-war new town in 1947, with the historic Old Village at its core. Just across the Clyde at Blantyre, the David Livingstone Birthplace at Shuttle Row tells the explorer's story from a textile-mill tenement, drawing visitors into the wider South Lanarkshire heritage and events calendar.

The visitor trade rests on hotels and guest houses across the town and the EK shopping centre, one of Scotland's largest indoor centres with an ice rink and cinema, alongside guides working the country parks. Rail links and the M74 carry day-trippers in from Glasgow, and the surrounding draws of Hamilton, Rutherglen and Glasgow feed a steady seasonal flow into East Kilbride.

South Shields.region: South Shields and the South Tyneside coast
South Shields.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the South Tyneside coast
s1loc: South Shields stretches along six miles of award-winning coastline at the mouth of the River Tyne, with golden Sandhaven Beach and the dramatic Marsden Beach below towering cliffs and the famous Marsden Rock sea stack. The National Trust's Souter Lighthouse, opened in 1871 as the world's first lighthouse built to be powered by electricity, stands as the coast's signature landmark above the North Sea.

The leisure and activity layer is led by Ocean Beach Pleasure Park behind Sandhaven, with the Pirate Ship, Waltzer, Dodgems and Log Flume among more than thirty rides. The cliffside Marsden Grotto, carved into the rock in the 1780s, the seafront promenade and the coastal paths of the Leas keep family and activity operators busy through the warmer months and beyond.

Heritage and culture run deep, from the UNESCO-listed Arbeia Roman Fort with its reconstructed West Gate and barrack rooms to South Shields Museum and Art Gallery, telling the borough's maritime and industrial story. The Word, the National Centre for the Written Word, holds 70,000 books, while the Customs House theatre by the ferry landing at Mill Dam and the summer This is South Tyneside Festival fill the events calendar.

The visitor trade draws on seafront hotels and guest houses, with guides running coastal and Roman tours and the seven-minute Shields Ferry linking across the Tyne to North Shields. The Tyne and Wear Metro reaches South Shields from Newcastle in about 25 minutes via the 2019 transport interchange, and the surrounding draws of Jarrow, North Shields and Tynemouth feed a strong seasonal flow.

Burton-on-Trent.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of brewing-town Burton
s1loc: Burton-on-Trent is the brewing capital of Britain, and the National Brewery Centre beside the historic Bass site tells that story with a working steam engine, vintage vehicles, a micro brewery, shire horses and tastings of ales brewed on site. The town's water from the River Trent valley made Bass and Worthington household names, and the brewing-heritage walking tours around the old breweries draw visitors into the marquee local draw.

The leisure and activity layer spreads out to Branston Water Park, a lakeside nature reserve with level trails, a visitor centre and birdwatching beside the Trent and Mersey Canal. The Washlands wetland along the River Trent offers footpaths and cycle routes alive with herons and kingfishers, and shire-horse carriage rides at the brewery quarter give family and activity operators a steady seasonal draw.

Heritage and culture centre on Claymills Victorian Pumping Station, a beautifully preserved nineteenth-century works that raises steam on selected days with vintage car days, steampunk gatherings and Professor Pumpernickel shows. The Brewing Heritage Festival and the Burton Ale Trail through the town's pubs and breweries fill the events calendar, set against a townscape shaped by its world-famous brewing past.

The visitor trade rests on hotels and inns across the town, including the Three Queens, with guides leading brewing-heritage and pumping-station tours. Burton-on-Trent railway station on the Cross Country line and easy reach of the A38 and M42 carry day-trippers in, and the surrounding draws of Tamworth, Lichfield and Derby feed a steady seasonal flow into east Staffordshire.

Shrewsbury.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of medieval Shrewsbury
s1loc: Shrewsbury sits within a great loop of the River Severn, its medieval streets crowned by Shrewsbury Castle, the red sandstone fortress raised by Roger de Montgomery in 1070 and now home to the Shropshire Regimental Museum. Thomas Telford's Gothic Laura's Tower stands on the original Norman motte, while the Benedictine Shrewsbury Abbey, founded in 1083, anchors the town's marquee heritage draw beside the river.

The leisure and activity layer gathers in The Quarry, a 29-acre riverside park dating from 1719 whose Dingle gardens were created by the celebrated horticulturalist Percy Thrower. Sabrina boat trips glide along the Severn, the riverside paths and weir draw walkers, and the open countryside of the Shropshire Hills beyond town gives activity and outdoor operators a varied seasonal offer across the year.

Heritage and culture run through more than 600 listed buildings, the timber-framed Tudor houses of Fish Street and Butcher Row, and Shrewsbury Museum and Art Gallery in the former Music Hall on The Square. Charles Darwin was born here and baptised at St Chad's, traced along the Darwin Trail, while the Shrewsbury Folk Festival and Flower Show fill a busy events calendar.

The visitor trade draws on town-centre hotels and guest houses, including Darwin's Townhouse, with guides leading abbey, castle and Tudor walking tours. Shrewsbury railway station links to Birmingham, Cardiff and the Cambrian Coast, and good roads carry day-trippers in, while the surrounding draws of Telford, Oswestry and Stafford feed a steady seasonal flow into the county town.

Rugby.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Rugby and east Warwickshire
s1loc: Rugby gave its name to a world sport, and the Webb Ellis Rugby Football Museum sits in the town-centre workshop where rugby balls have been made by hand since 1842. The story traces back to Rugby School, founded in 1567, where in 1823 William Webb Ellis is said to have first picked up the ball and run with it, making the town the marquee draw for sporting pilgrims worldwide.

The leisure and activity layer is led by Draycote Water, a reservoir and country park a few miles out with a five-mile circular path for walking, cycling and jogging, plus sailing, windsurfing and fishing on the open water. Caldecott Park in the town centre and Coombe Abbey Country Park towards Coventry add family days out, giving activity operators a steady seasonal draw across the warmer months.

Heritage and culture centre on the Rugby Art Gallery and Museum, whose collection includes finds from the Romano-British town of Tripontium on the old Watling Street. The Gunpowder Plot link to Coombe Abbey, the chapel and quadrangles of Rugby School and a calendar of events at the Benn Hall, opened by the Queen Mother in 1961, give guides and cultural operators a distinct local narrative.

The visitor trade draws on hotels such as the Draycote Hotel and Whitefields Golf Club, with guides working the rugby heritage and the country parks. Rugby railway station is a principal stop on the West Coast Main Line, with frequent trains to London Euston and Birmingham, and easy reach of the M6 and M1 carries day-trippers in alongside Nuneaton, Coventry and Daventry.

Stafford.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the county town of Stafford
s1loc: Stafford built its visitor appeal on Stafford Castle, first raised by William the Conqueror and dominating the skyline for over 900 years with free entry and views across four counties. In the town centre, the Ancient High House of 1595 is England's largest timber-framed Elizabethan town house, where King Charles I stayed in 1642, now a museum dressed in authentic interiors from different periods.

The leisure and activity layer runs through Victoria Park beside the River Sow, a yearly Green Flag winner enhanced by Heritage Lottery projects, and out to Shugborough Estate, the National Trust's sweeping parkland and riverside gardens. Shugborough's servants' quarters and Park Farm animals, plus the walking and cycling routes of Cannock Chase nearby, give family and activity operators a strong seasonal draw across the year.

Heritage and culture centre on the Stafford Gatehouse Theatre and its MET Studio, home to the acclaimed Stafford Festival Shakespeare, with the historic town centre and its medieval and Georgian streets telling the county-town story. Shugborough as ancestral home of the Earls of Lichfield, the castle's living-history events and a busy festival calendar give guides and cultural operators plenty of local material across the seasons.

The visitor trade draws on town-centre and out-of-town hotels and guest houses, with guides leading castle, Ancient High House and Shugborough tours. Stafford railway station on the West Coast Main Line and easy reach of the M6 carry day-trippers in, and the surrounding draws of Cannock, Stoke-on-Trent and Telford feed a steady seasonal flow into the county town.

Taunton.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the county town of Somerset
s1loc: Taunton, the county town of Somerset, centres its visitor appeal on the Museum of Somerset, housed within the twelfth-century walls of Taunton Castle in the town centre with free entry. Its treasures include a 200-million-year-old plesiosaur fossil, the Low Ham Roman mosaic, the Frome Hoard of Roman coins and a Bronze Age gold torc, making the castle the marquee heritage draw for visitors to the levels.

The leisure and activity layer is led by Vivary Park just off the town centre, with a large adventure play area, tree trail, tennis courts, a pay-and-play golf course, mini golf and the Vivary Adventure and High Ropes Centre. Riverside walks along the River Tone, the open countryside of the Quantock Hills and seasonal agricultural shows give family and activity operators a varied draw across the year.

Heritage and culture run through the Taunton Brewhouse on the banks of the Tone, the largest theatre and arts centre in town, with a 352-seat auditorium and studio set in the Georgian Old Brewery house of 1977. Hestercombe House and Gardens blends Georgian and Victorian landscapes with outdoor Shakespeare, and cricket at the County Ground, home of Somerset County Cricket Club, fills the events calendar.

The visitor trade draws on town-centre hotels and guest houses, with guides working the castle, the Tone waterfront and the Quantocks. Taunton railway station on the Great Western main line and the M5 motorway carry day-trippers in from across the South West, and the surrounding draws of Bridgwater, Yeovil and Frome feed a steady seasonal flow into the county town.
